To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) we propose a framework for representing competencies in mathematics and (2) we show how these competencies are used for different purposes.
the competency ontology enables interoperability and reusability of learning objects in mathematics.

we propose a competency ontology that is based on a taxonomy of knowledge components and cognitive processes, which can be used in different ways, e.g. for the design and reuse of learning objects, and that the ontology can be used for interoperability.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a systematic approach to competency modeling and a standardization of competencies in mathematics.
developing a general framework of competencies and a method of their determination.
a systematic approach of determining competencies in mathematics and their reuse in different learning environments.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
we have developed an approach to competences represented as pairs of cognitive process and knowledge that can be reused across domains and that are interoperable.
the approach is a first step towards interoperable and comparable learning objects.
the approach is promising and that the proposed competencies can be used to characterize learning objects in mathematics and to enable interoperable learning.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have created an approach to competences that can be applied to different learning environments and domains and that is interoperable and reusable.
we propose an approach how to describe learning objects in terms of competencies.
we have developed a framework for representing competencies and we have shown how to use this framework to represent competencies in a particular domain, i.e. mathematics.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is possible to create a common ontology for competencies, which is reusable and can be used for different purposes in different contexts.
the competencies are not domain dependent, but rather domain independent and therefore reusable.

we have shown that the cognitive process ontology can be used for different purposes, e.g., to describe learning objects, to predict students' behavior, to improve curricula and as a quasi-standard for interoperability.
